newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sees '96 growth 4.5-4.6 pct - Bear Stearns.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sees '96 growth 4.5-4.6 pct - Bear Stearns.

text.p: Mexico's finance minister Guillermo Ortiz told a group of economists on Tuesday that he expects 1996 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of between 4.5 and 4.6 percent, Bear Stearns said.
Bear Stearns economist David Malpass, citing his notes of Ortiz's presentation, said in a report that Ortiz expected Q4 1996 growth of five to six percent.
Ortiz also predicted December inflation of more than three percent, due partly to an increase in Metro subway fares, and January inflation of two percent or below, Bear Stearns said.
Bear Stearns said Ortiz stuck to the government's announced growth expectation of four percent in 1997, with inflation of 15 percent.

The report said Ortiz expected growth in 1997 to come mainly from investment and consumption, with consumption growing 2.0-2.5 percent in real terms but still not attaining 1994 levels for two more years.
Malpass quoted Ortiz as saying the current account deficit, which was $250 million through September, might rise to $1.0 billion-$1.2 billion for 1996.
The report said Ortiz saw a possibility of pre-paying existing debt to the IMF and the United States and taking out an extended fund facility with the IMF, though Mexico might not then draw upon it.
It also said that Ortiz wanted a 10 percent real increase in tax revenues in 1997, including improved value-added tax collection. Monthly tax revenues had been rising strongly in recent months.

On monetary policy, the report said Ortiz said the central bank's programme for 1997, due soon, could increase the monetary base by 23-25 percent, comprising 15 percent inflation, four percent growth and a moderate remonetisation.
